reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ATS-ERS
clinicalPearls: Results from accumulation of surfactant-derived lipoproteinaceous material within alveoli because of impaired clearance by alveolar macrophages
The most common (autoimmune) form is caused by neutralising autoantibodies against granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF)
Presents insidiously with breathlessness and dry cough, often with signs milder than the radiographic appearance would suggest
High-resolution CT classically shows a crazy-paving pattern of ground-glass opacity superimposed on interlobular septal thickening, often in a geographic distribution
Bronchoalveolar lavage returns characteristically milky, opaque fluid that stains strongly with periodic acid-Schiff
A positive serum anti-GM-CSF antibody test confirms the autoimmune subtype and distinguishes it from hereditary and secondary forms
Whole-lung lavage remains the principal treatment for symptomatic disease, physically washing out the accumulated material
Because surfactant impairs local defence, patients are predisposed to secondary infection, including with opportunistic organisms such as Nocardia
reference.pathophysiology: In pulmonary alveolar proteinosis the alveoli fill with excess surfactant components (phospholipids and surfactant proteins) that alveolar macrophages are unable to catabolise and clear. In the autoimmune form, autoantibodies neutralise GM-CSF, a cytokine required for macrophage maturation and surfactant clearance, leaving macrophages functionally deficient. Hereditary forms arise from mutations affecting the GM-CSF receptor, and secondary forms occur when macrophage number or function is impaired by haematological disease, inhaled dusts, or immunosuppression. The alveolar filling creates a diffusion barrier producing hypoxaemia and restrictive physiology.
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution CT of the chest to identify the crazy-paving pattern
Bronchoalveolar lavage with cytology and PAS staining
Pulmonary function testing showing restriction and reduced diffusing capacity
Evaluation for secondary causes and opportunistic infection when clinically indicated
Surgical lung biopsy only if less invasive testing is inconclusive
redFlags: Rapidly worsening hypoxaemia or respiratory failure requiring urgent intervention
Superimposed infection presenting as fever and clinical deterioration, including opportunistic pathogens
New systemic illness suggesting an underlying haematological malignancy driving a secondary form
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally favourable in autoimmune disease, which often responds well to whole-lung lavage though repeated procedures may be needed; secondary forms depend on the underlying condition, and a minority progress to fibrosis or fatal respiratory failure.
pitfalls: Attributing the striking radiographic findings to infection or pulmonary oedema and missing the diagnosis
Failing to check anti-GM-CSF antibodies to categorise the disease
Overlooking a superimposed opportunistic infection during clinical deterioration
Not investigating for an underlying haematological or occupational cause in secondary disease
